ingredients.preparation: chapssalgaru — the chew; substitute fine glutinous rice flour
about 40 °C — warm to the wrist, not hot

ingredients.item: neutral oil , worked into the dough
sunflower or pine nuts, coarsely chopped

ingredients.preparation: about 3 tbsp / 40 g total across the batch

instructions.heading: Shape the pockets with oiled hands, not floured ones
instructions.action: Shape the pockets with oiled hands, not floured ones. With wet or oiled palms, tear off a ball of dough (about 80 g), and flatten it in your hand into a 10 cm disc — the dough is too soft to roll; the palm is the rolling pin. A spoonful of filling (about 20 g) into the center, then the disc's edges gathered up and pinched closed like a drawstring purse, seam down on the plate. Eight of them.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: each purse is fully sealed with no sugar showing (an open seam leaks molten sugar straight into the oil — the batch's one real hazard, both for the fry and for the sugar lost from the pancake) and the dough around the filling is even, without a thin blowout side.

instructions.heading: Fry low and slow, flatten once
instructions.action: Fry low and slow, flatten once. A generously oiled pan at medium-low — the oil at a lazy shimmer, not a sizzle (around 160 °C if the pan could speak). Two or three purses in seam-side-down, 60–90 seconds to set the bottom, then flip and press each one flat with the spatula — one confident press into a 1.5 cm disc — and another 2–3 minutes on that side, flipping once more briefly to re-crisp the first face.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the crust goes deep golden and lacy-crisp at the pressed edges while the interior stays thick and pale-soft; press one at the center — it should give like a cushion. A dark crust at 90 seconds means the heat is running high and the filling inside is still grainy — the low-slow fry exists precisely so the sugar melts in the time the crust browns.

instructions.heading: Rest one minute — the safety minute — and serve
instructions.action: Rest one minute — the safety minute — and serve. Off the pan to a rack or plate, and a full minute before the first bite: the filling is molten syrup at 120 °C-plus straight from the pan, the street cart's small legend of burned mouths and burned fingers.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the eating test: the first bite tears the crisp crust and the syrup runs — dark brown sugar, cinnamon, the seeds' crunch, the chewy-soft interior catching it all. It should be slightly too hot, slightly messy, and completely worth both. That is the street cart's exact register, reproduced.

visualDonenessCues: The dough: wet, risen an hour to doubled, shaped with oiled hands, sealed purses.
The fry: medium-low (160 °C's lazy shimmer), pressed once to 1.5 cm, deep-gold crust, cushion-soft interior.
The melt: the filling fully liquid at the first tear, seeds suspended in the syrup.
The serve: the one-minute rest, then straight from the rack — hotteok has no second act.
storageNotes: Eats from the rack, full stop — see the Note. The dough keeps 24 hours refrigerated after the first rise (punch down, chill, warm 30 minutes before shaping); shaped purses 30 minutes under a damp towel.

Variations: the seed mix swaps freely; a spoon of cream cheese with the brown sugar for the modern carts' melted-cheese fork; the savory hotteok (scallion and soy) is a different cart's lunch — same dough, opposite filling, worth its own afternoon.
